name: Midface ratio

card.summary: A facial proportion comparing the width between the pupils to the vertical distance from pupils to lips, used in looksmaxxing to judge midface length and attractiveness.
card.note: Measurement conventions vary between communities and clinical papers.

quick.overview:
The midface ratio compares the distance between the pupils with the distance from the pupil line down to the lips. In looksmaxxing communities a ratio near 1:1 is described as ideal, with a longer midface (ratios around 0.9 or below) discussed as a flaw and a shorter one as a youthful or feminine trait.

People use it to decide which features to change, for example hairstyles, brow position, philtrum length or surgery. Clinical journals use a differently defined 'midface ratio' in eyelid surgery studies, so the term has more than one meaning.
quick.how: Members measure from a front-facing photo with the face level and neutral, using a tool or a drawn overlay, then post the number for opinions. Threads debate where to measure to, whether the upper lip or the lip line, and how to standardise it. Related discussions cover what changes the number, such as brow height and philtrum.
quick.risks: The measurement is easy to distort with camera angle and expression, and community threads disagree about which direction is better for men. Some users describe distress over small numbers; forum members themselves argue about how much it matters.

lead: The midface ratio is a facial proportion used in looksmaxxing to describe how long or short the middle of the face is. It is usually calculated by dividing the distance between the pupils by the vertical distance from the pupil line to the lips, with 1:1 treated as the benchmark [1][2].

Members use the number to judge the midface and to decide what might improve it. A longer midface (lower ratio) is often described as a defect, though some posters argue a ratio just under 1 can read as masculine [3]. Related features that members adjust or discuss include brow height, philtrum length and the lower face [2][4].

A separate use of the term appears in plastic surgery papers, where a midface ratio compares brow-to-lower-eyelid and lower-eyelid-to-nose-base lengths. Studies in Asian patients measured how eyelid procedures change that ratio [5][6].

angle.text: People use the ratio as a diagnostic for the midface and then look at ways to shift how long the midface appears, such as brow position or cosmetic procedures.

infobox: Interpupillary distance divided by pupil-to-lip distance

paras: In forum usage the ratio divides interpupillary distance by the vertical distance from the pupil line to the lips. Threads disagree on the lip landmark: one asks whether the middle or upper lip should be used, and others propose standardising measurement alongside the facial width-to-height ratio [7][8]. Posters sometimes use the eye-mouth-eye angle as an alternative way to describe the midface [1][3].

One looksmax.org post argues that 1:1 is not necessary, that men tend to have longer midfaces than women, and that a ratio above 1 reads as boyish; another post says a ratio around 0.95 can look better than above 1 on faces with strong craniofacial development [1][3]. Others ask whether ratios like 0.9 are damaging and whether higher brows or supraorbital features could compensate [9]. Other threads argue the main cause of a long-looking face is something other than the ratio and debate whether the ratio matters at all [4][10].

Plastic surgery papers use a different midface ratio. A 2018 study measured the ratio of brow-to-lower-eyelid length to lower-eyelid-to-nasal-base length before and after levator aponeurosis folding for upper lid ptosis in 21 patients, comparing it with 20 Chinese film stars [5]. A 2022 study of 45 young Asian women found upper eyelid blepharoplasty moved facial width proportion and midface ratio closer to the golden ratio [6]. An older paper used a theoretical midface ratio to describe midface prognathism in Binder's syndrome [11]. An anthropometric comparison of painted portraits looked at proportions in beautiful women, femmes fatales and artists' mothers [12].

No studies found on the pupil-to-lip midface ratio as used in looksmaxxing communities. Related clinical studies of a differently defined midface ratio after eyelid surgery are described above [5][6].

lore.intro: The midface ratio is a staple of face-rating threads on looksmax.org, where members post measurements and debate which values are ideal [1][3][9].

claims.claim: A midface ratio of about 1:1 is ideal and lower is a flaw
claims.believers: Members describe a longer midface (such as 0.9) as a problem and ask whether features like high-set brows can compensate [9][10].
claims.experts: No published study has validated a 1:1 pupil-to-lip ratio as an attractiveness standard; clinical papers use a differently defined midface ratio [5][6].

claims.claim: A slightly longer midface can look more masculine
claims.believers: Posters argue men naturally have longer midfaces and a ratio near 0.95 can look better than one above 1 [1][3].
claims.experts: No published study cited here has tested this claim.
